message.content:
I don’t have a way to probe your connection from here, but you can quickly find out your current download/upload speeds yourself. Below are a few easy options you can try on a Windows machine:

---

## 1. Use the official Speedtest CLI (recommended)

If you have **Python** installed, you can install the Speedtest CLI tool and run a test from the command line.

```powershell
# Install the Speedtest CLI package
pip install speedtest-cli

# Run a speed test
speedtest
```

The output will show you:

- **Download speed** (in Mbps)
- **Upload speed** (in Mbps)
- **Ping** (latency)

If you prefer a more detailed report, you can add `--verbose`:

```powershell
speedtest --verbose
```

---

## 2. Use PowerShell’s built‑in `Invoke-WebRequest` (quick & no extra installs)

This method downloads a known file from a public server and measures how long it takes. It’s a rough estimate but works if you don’t have `speedtest-cli`.

```powershell
$uri = "https://speedtest.tele2.net/10MB.zip"
$dest = "$env:TEMP\10MB.zip"

$sw = [System.Diagnostics.Stopwatch]::StartNew()
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri $uri -OutFile $dest
$sw.Stop()

$bytes = (Get-Item $dest).Length
$seconds = $sw.Elapsed.TotalSeconds
$mbps = ($bytes * 8) / ($seconds * 1e6)

Write-Host "Download speed: $([math]::Round($mbps,2)) Mbps"
```

> **Tip:** Delete the downloaded file afterward:
> ```powershell
> Remove-Item $dest
> ```

---

## 3. Use a web browser

If you prefer a graphical interface, simply visit one of the following sites:

- [speedtest.net](https://www.speedtest.net/)
- [fast.com](https://fast.com/) (Netflix’s speed test)
- [speedof.me](https://speedof.me/)

Click “Go” or “Start Test” and the site will automatically measure your download/upload speeds and ping.

---

## 4. Quick one‑liner with `curl` (if you have it)

If you have `curl` installed (Windows 10+ includes it by default), you can do:

```powershell
curl -o NUL https://speedtest.tele2.net/10MB.zip
```

This will download the file to `/dev/null` (or `NUL` on Windows) and you can time it manually with PowerShell’s stopwatch as shown above.

---

### What to look for

| Metric | Typical values (good home broadband) |
|--------|--------------------------------------|
| **Download** | 25 – 100 Mbps (or higher for fiber) |
| **Upload**   | 5 – 20 Mbps (or higher for fiber) |
| **Ping**     | < 50 ms (gaming/VoIP) |

If your numbers are far below what your ISP advertises, you might want to:

1. Restart your modem/router.
2. Check for firmware updates.
3. Run tests at different times of day to see if congestion is the issue.
4. Contact your ISP if the problem persists.

---

Let me know if you’d like help installing `speedtest-cli`, interpreting the results, or troubleshooting any issues you find!
